meaning: The resource that is fully used while the rest of the machine is partly idle. It is the resource a job runs out of first.
A set of hardware counters inside a processor core. Each counter counts one kind of event, such as a clock cycle or a retired micro-operation.

The record of one workload on one machine. It gives the throughput, where the CPU's slots went, what lies behind the largest loss, the GPU readings when a GPU does the work, and how everything was counted.
The Linux tool that reads the processor's counters. The perf stat command runs a program and prints the counter totals.

What perf does when it cannot count every requested event at the same time. The events take turns, perf scales each count up to the whole run, and it reports the share of the measurement time during which each counter was running.
One of the smaller internal steps that a core splits each program instruction into. Intel writes it as uOp.
The number of finished instructions divided by the number of clock cycles. It shows how much work a core did per cycle, but not why the rest of its capacity went unused.
The stages of a core's pipeline that predict which instructions come next, fetch them and decode them into micro-operations.
The stages of a core's pipeline that execute micro-operations in the arithmetic and memory units, out of program order when that is faster.
The last pipeline stage. It makes the results of executed micro-operations final, in program order.
The pipeline stage that separates a core's front end from its back end. Arm counts slots at this stage.
Fetching and executing the instructions after a branch on a guess, before the core knows which way the branch goes.
Throwing away the micro-operations started after a wrong branch guess, and restarting from the right place.
One chance, in one clock cycle, to pass one micro-operation from the front end to the back end. A core has a fixed number of slots per cycle.
A core's number of slots per cycle, for example 10 on the Cortex-X925 and Neoverse V3 and 5 on the Cortex-A725.
A method from a 2014 Intel paper. It sorts every slot of every cycle into one of four buckets to show how a core used its capacity.
The share of slots that carried a micro-operation which finished and was kept. It measures the core's useful work.
The share of slots that carried work thrown away after a wrong branch guess. In the corrected formulas, it also includes the slots lost while the core recovers from the wrong guess.
The share of slots left empty because the front end had no micro-operation ready.
The share of slots left empty because the back end could not accept another micro-operation.

The share of back-end bound slots in which the core waits for data to be loaded or stored. Faster memory helps such a job: more bandwidth if its loads stream through memory, and lower latency if each load waits for the one before.
The share of back-end bound slots in which the execution units are busy or operations wait on each other's results. A faster core helps such a job, and faster memory does not.
The share of cycles in which the back end waited on memory, counted by a separate event.
Two Arm events. OP_SPEC counts the micro-operations dispatched through a slot, including those later thrown away, and OP_RETIRED counts the micro-operations that retired.
The Arm event that counts empty slots. It is the sum of STALL_SLOT_FRONTEND and STALL_SLOT_BACKEND.
Arm's per-core adjustment that moves the slots lost while recovering from a flush out of front-end bound and into bad speculation.
The Arm event that counts the cycles the front end spent recovering from a flush. The formulas for the Neoverse V3, Cortex-X925 and Cortex-A725 use it.
Two hardware threads sharing one processor core. AMD's top-down analysis adds a bucket for the slots lost to the other thread.
The Arm processors that AWS designs for EC2. Graviton2, 3, 4 and 5 use the Neoverse N1, V1, V2 and V3 cores.
NVIDIA's desktop machine with a GB10 GPU and two types of Arm core, the larger Cortex-X925 and the smaller Cortex-A725.
NVIDIA's small onboard computer for robots, with Cortex-A78AE cores. Arm publishes no top-down file for that core.
A physics simulator. The sample card records one core stepping a MuJoCo humanoid model, which stands in for the arm's simulation.
An EC2 instance with no virtual machine layer between the operating system and the hardware.
A function launched on the GPU, such as a matrix multiply. It is unrelated to the operating system's kernel.
The GPU's basic processing unit. A GPU chip contains many of them.
Units inside each SM with a pipeline of their own for matrix multiply-accumulate instructions, the arithmetic of training and inference.
The GPU units that find what each camera ray hits when an image is rendered. We found no counter for them in the documentation of nvidia-smi, DCGM, tegrastats or Nsight Compute.
The percent of time in the sample period during which at least one kernel was running on the GPU. It says nothing about how much of the GPU the kernel used.
The Jetson's always-on monitor. It reports the GPU's activation time, the memory bandwidth in use at the memory controller and the power drawn on each power rail.
NVIDIA's fleet monitoring service. It reports SM activity, tensor activity and memory activity for each GPU.
The fraction of time during which at least one group of threads was active on a GPU's SMs, averaged over all SMs. Threads waiting on memory count as active.
The fraction of cycles during which the GPU's tensor pipeline was active.
NVIDIA's profiler that puts the CPU samples, GPU calls and kernels of one application on a single timeline.
NVIDIA's profiler for a single GPU kernel. It reports the kernel's throughput against the GPU's maximum and draws a roofline chart.
A chart of a kernel's achieved speed against its arithmetic per byte of memory moved. The sloped part of the roof is the memory bandwidth limit, and the flat part is the peak compute limit.
The second level of top-down analysis, which splits back-end bound into memory bound and core bound. Arm's files for the Neoverse V3, Cortex-X925 and Cortex-A725 define it with events of their own.

The GPU's general floating-point path on the ordinary CUDA cores, as opposed to the tensor pipeline. SIMT stands for single instruction, multiple threads. We read a kernel name that contains simt as a kernel that did its arithmetic on this path.
The PyTorch setting that decides whether a float32 matrix multiply may be computed in a narrower format. The default, "highest", keeps float32, and "high" allows TensorFloat32.
A number format that stores 10 mantissa bits where float32 stores 23. PyTorch may use it for a float32 matrix multiply when the precision setting is "high".

The section of a kernel profile that reports compute and memory throughput. Each figure is the highest of the percentages reported by the counters behind it, so it need not be a share of the chip's peak arithmetic rate or memory bandwidth.
